change_shape_to(a, newshape, order='C'):
    Gives a new shape to an numset without changing its data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Array to be change_shape_tod.
    newshape : int or tuple of ints
        The new shape should be compatible with the original shape. If
        an integer, then the result will be a 1-D numset of that length.
        One shape dimension can be -1. In this case, the value is
        inferred from the length of the numset and remaining dimensions.
    order : {'C', 'F', 'A'}, optional
        Read the elements of `a` using this index order, and place the
        elements into the change_shape_tod numset using this index order.  'C'
        averages to read / write the elements using C-like index order,
        with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first
        axis index changing slowest. 'F' averages to read / write the
        elements using Fortran-like index order, with the first index
        changing fastest, and the last index changing slowest. Note that
        the 'C' and 'F' options take no account of the memory layout of
        the underlying numset, and only refer to the order of indexing.
        'A' averages to read / write the elements in Fortran-like index
        order if `a` is Fortran *contiguous* in memory, C-like order
        otherwise.

    Returns
    -------
    change_shape_tod_numset : ndnumset
        This will be a new view object if possible; otherwise, it will
        be a copy.  Note there is no guarantee of the *memory layout* (C- or
        Fortran- contiguous) of the returned numset.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.change_shape_to : Equivalent method.

    Notes
    -----
    It is not always possible to change the shape of an numset without
    copying the data. If you want an error to be raised when the data is copied,
    you should assign the new shape to the shape attribute of the numset::

     >>> a = bn.zeros((10, 2))

     # A switching_places makes the numset non-contiguous
     >>> b = a.T

     # Taking a view makes it possible to modify the shape without modifying
     # the initial object.
     >>> c = b.view()
     >>> c.shape = (20)
     Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
     AttributeError: Incompatible shape for in-place modification. Use
     `.change_shape_to()` to make a copy with the desired shape.

    The `order` keyword gives the index ordering both for *fetching* the values
    from `a`, and then *placing* the values into the output numset.
    For example, let's say you have an numset:

    >>> a = bn.arr_range(6).change_shape_to((3, 2))
    >>> a
    numset([[0, 1],
           [2, 3],
           [4, 5]])

    You can think of reshaping as first asviewing the numset (using the given
    index order), then sticking the elements from the asviewed numset into the
    new numset using the same kind of index ordering as was used for the
    asviewing.

    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3)) # C-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a), (2, 3)) # equivalent to C asview then C change_shape_to
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3), order='F') # Fortran-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a, order='F'), (2, 3), order='F')
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])

numset(obj, itemsize=None, copy=True, unicode=None, order=None):
    Create a `charnumset`.

    .. note::
       This class is provided for numnumset backward-compatibility.
       New code (not concerned with numnumset compatibility) should use
       numsets of type `string_` or `unicode_` and use the free functions
       in :mod:`beatnum.char <beatnum.core.defcharnumset>` for fast
       vectorisationd string operations instead.

    Versus a regular NumPy numset of type `str` or `unicode`, this
    class adds the following functionality:

      1) values automatically have whitespace removed from the end
         when indexed

      2) comparison operators automatically remove whitespace from the
         end when comparing values

      3) vectorisationd string operations are provided as methods
         (e.g. `str.endswith`) and infix operators (e.g. ``+, *, %``)

    Parameters
    ----------
    obj : numset of str or unicode-like

    itemsize : int, optional
        `itemsize` is the number of characters per scalar in the
        resulting numset.  If `itemsize` is None, and `obj` is an
        object numset or a Python list, the `itemsize` will be
        automatically deterget_mined.  If `itemsize` is provided and `obj`
        is of type str or unicode, then the `obj` string will be
        chunked into `itemsize` pieces.

    copy : bool, optional
        If true (default), then the object is copied.  Otherwise, a copy
        will only be made if __numset__ returns a copy, if obj is a
        nested sequence, or if a copy is needed to satisfy any_condition of the other
        requirements (`itemsize`, unicode, `order`, etc.).

    unicode : bool, optional
        When true, the resulting `charnumset` can contain Unicode
        characters, when false only 8-bit characters.  If unicode is
        None and `obj` is one of the following:

          - a `charnumset`,
          - an ndnumset of type `str` or `unicode`
          - a Python str or unicode object,

        then the unicode setting of the output numset will be
        automatically deterget_mined.

    order : {'C', 'F', 'A'}, optional
        Specify the order of the numset.  If order is 'C' (default), then the
        numset will be in C-contiguous order (last-index varies the
        fastest).  If order is 'F', then the returned numset
        will be in Fortran-contiguous order (first-index varies the
        fastest).  If order is 'A', then the returned numset may
        be in any_condition order (either C-, Fortran-contiguous, or even
        discontiguous).

arr_range(*args, **params):arr_range([start,] stop[, step,], dtype=None, *, like=None)

    Return evenly spaced values within a given interval.

    Values are generated within the half-open interval ``[start, stop)``
    (in other words, the interval including `start` but excluding `stop`).
    For integer arguments the function is equivalent to the Python built-in
    `range` function, but returns an ndnumset rather than a list.

    When using a non-integer step, such as 0.1, the results will often not
    be consistent.  It is better to use `beatnum.linspace` for these cases.

    Parameters
    ----------
    start : integer or reality, optional
        Start of interval.  The interval includes this value.  The default
        start value is 0.
    stop : integer or reality
        End of interval.  The interval does not include this value, except
        in some cases filter_condition `step` is not an integer and floating point
        round-off affects the length of `out`.
    step : integer or reality, optional
        Spacing between values.  For any_condition output `out`, this is the distance
        between two adjacent values, ``out[i+1] - out[i]``.  The default
        step size is 1.  If `step` is specified as a position argument,
        `start` must also be given.
    dtype : dtype
        The type of the output numset.  If `dtype` is not given, infer the data
        type from the other ibnut arguments.
    like : numset_like
        Reference object to allow the creation of numsets which are not
        NumPy numsets. If an numset-like passed in as ``like`` supports
        the ``__numset_function__`` protocol, the result will be defined
        by it. In this case, it ensures the creation of an numset object
        compatible with that passed in via this argument.

        .. versionadded:: 1.20.0

    Returns
    -------
    arr_range : ndnumset
        Array of evenly spaced values.

        For floating point arguments, the length of the result is
        ``ceil((stop - start)/step)``.  Because of floating point overflow,
        this rule may result in the last element of `out` being greater
        than `stop`.

    See Also
    --------
    beatnum.linspace : Evenly spaced numbers with careful handling of endpoints.
    beatnum.ogrid: Arrays of evenly spaced numbers in N-dimensions.
    beatnum.mgrid: Grid-shaped numsets of evenly spaced numbers in N-dimensions.

pad_diagonal(a, val, wrap=False):Fill the main diagonal of the given numset of any_condition dimensionality.

    For an numset `a` with ``a.ndim >= 2``, the diagonal is the list of
    locations with indices ``a[i, ..., i]`` total identical. This function
    modifies the ibnut numset in-place, it does not return a value.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset, at least 2-D.
      Array whose diagonal is to be masked_fill, it gets modified in-place.

    val : scalar or numset_like
      Value(s) to write on the diagonal. If `val` is scalar, the value is
      written along the diagonal. If numset-like, the convert_into_one_dimed `val` is
      written along the diagonal, duplicateing if necessary to fill total
      diagonal entries.

    wrap : bool
      For tall matrices in NumPy version up to 1.6.2, the
      diagonal "wrapped" after N columns. You can have this behavior
      with this option. This affects only tall matrices.

    See also
    --------
    diag_indices, diag_indices_from

    Notes
    -----
    .. versionadded:: 1.4.0

    This functionality can be obtained via `diag_indices`, but internally
    this version uses a much faster implementation that never constructs the
    indices and uses simple slicing.

any_condition(a, axis=None, out=None, keepdims=<no value>, *, where=<no value>):
    Test whether any_condition numset element along a given axis evaluates to True.

    Returns single boolean unless `axis` is not ``None``

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Ibnut numset or object that can be converted to an numset.
    axis : None or int or tuple of ints, optional
        Axis or axes along which a logical OR reduction is performed.
        The default (``axis=None``) is to perform a logical OR over all
        the dimensions of the ibnut numset. `axis` may be negative, in
        which case it counts from the last to the first axis.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

        If this is a tuple of ints, a reduction is performed on multiple
        axes, instead of a single axis or all the axes as before.
    out : ndnumset, optional
        Alternate output numset in which to place the result.  It must have
        the same shape as the expected output and its type is preserved
        (e.g., if it is of type float, then it will remain so, returning
        1.0 for True and 0.0 for False, regardless of the type of `a`).
        See :ref:`ufuncs-output-type` for more details.

    keepdims : bool, optional
        If this is set to True, the axes which are reduced are left
        in the result as dimensions with size one. With this option,
        the result will broadcast correctly against the ibnut numset.

        If the default value is passed, then `keepdims` will not be
        passed through to the `any_condition` method of sub-classes of
        `ndnumset`, however any_condition non-default value will be.  If the
        sub-class' method does not implement `keepdims` any_condition
        exceptions will be raised.

    filter_condition : numset_like of bool, optional
        Elements to include in checking for any_condition `True` values.
        See `~beatnum.ufunc.reduce` for details.

        .. versionadded:: 1.20.0

    Returns
    -------
    any_condition : bool or ndnumset
        A new boolean or `ndnumset` is returned unless `out` is specified,
        in which case a reference to `out` is returned.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.any_condition : equivalent method

    total : Test whether total elements along a given axis evaluate to True.

    Notes
    -----
    Not a Number (NaN), positive infinity and negative infinity evaluate
    to `True` because these are not equal to zero.

difference(a, n=1, axis=-1, prepend=<no value>, apd=<no value>):
    Calculate the n-th discrete differenceerence along the given axis.

    The first differenceerence is given by ``out[i] = a[i+1] - a[i]`` along
    the given axis, higher differenceerences are calculated by using `difference`
    recursively.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Ibnut numset
    n : int, optional
        The number of times values are differenceerenced. If zero, the ibnut
        is returned as-is.
    axis : int, optional
        The axis along which the differenceerence is taken, default is the
        last axis.
    prepend, apd : numset_like, optional
        Values to prepend or apd to `a` along axis prior to
        perforget_ming the differenceerence.  Scalar values are expanded to
        numsets with length 1 in the direction of axis and the shape
        of the ibnut numset in along all other axes.  Otherwise the
        dimension and shape must match `a` except along axis.

        .. versionadded:: 1.16.0

    Returns
    -------
    difference : ndnumset
        The n-th differenceerences. The shape of the output is the same as `a`
        except along `axis` filter_condition the dimension is smaller by `n`. The
        type of the output is the same as the type of the differenceerence
        between any_condition two elements of `a`. This is the same as the type of
        `a` in most cases. A notable exception is `datetime64`, which
        results in a `timedelta64` output numset.

    See Also
    --------
    gradient, edifference1d, cumsum

    Notes
    -----
    Type is preserved for boolean numsets, so the result will contain
    `False` when consecutive elements are the same and `True` when they
    differenceer.

    For unsigned integer numsets, the results will also be unsigned. This
    should not be surprising, as the result is consistent with
    calculating the differenceerence directly:

    >>> u8_arr = bn.numset([1, 0], dtype=bn.uint8)
    >>> bn.difference(u8_arr)
    numset([255], dtype=uint8)
    >>> u8_arr[1,...] - u8_arr[0,...]
    255

    If this is not desirable, then the numset should be cast to a larger
    integer type first:

    >>> i16_arr = u8_arr.convert_type(bn.int16)
    >>> bn.difference(i16_arr)
    numset([-1], dtype=int16)

uniq(ar, return_index=False, return_inverse=False, return_counts=False, axis=None):
    Find the uniq elements of an numset.

    Returns the sorted uniq elements of an numset. There are three optional
    outputs in addition to the uniq elements:

    * the indices of the ibnut numset that give the uniq values
    * the indices of the uniq numset that reconstruct the ibnut numset
    * the number of times each uniq value comes up in the ibnut numset

    Parameters
    ----------
    ar : numset_like
        Ibnut numset. Unless `axis` is specified, this will be convert_into_one_dimed if it
        is not already 1-D.
    return_index : bool, optional
        If True, also return the indices of `ar` (along the specified axis,
        if provided, or in the convert_into_one_dimed numset) that result in the uniq numset.
    return_inverseerse : bool, optional
        If True, also return the indices of the uniq numset (for the specified
        axis, if provided) that can be used to reconstruct `ar`.
    return_counts : bool, optional
        If True, also return the number of times each uniq item appears
        in `ar`.

        .. versionadded:: 1.9.0

    axis : int or None, optional
        The axis to operate on. If None, `ar` will be convert_into_one_dimed. If an integer,
        the subnumsets indexed by the given axis will be convert_into_one_dimed and treated
        as the elements of a 1-D numset with the dimension of the given axis,
        see the notes for more details.  Object numsets or structured numsets
        that contain objects are not supported if the `axis` kwarg is used. The
        default is None.

        .. versionadded:: 1.13.0

    Returns
    -------
    uniq : ndnumset
        The sorted uniq values.
    uniq_indices : ndnumset, optional
        The indices of the first occurrences of the uniq values in the
        original numset. Only provided if `return_index` is True.
    uniq_inverseerse : ndnumset, optional
        The indices to reconstruct the original numset from the
        uniq numset. Only provided if `return_inverseerse` is True.
    uniq_counts : ndnumset, optional
        The number of times each of the uniq values comes up in the
        original numset. Only provided if `return_counts` is True.

        .. versionadded:: 1.9.0

    See Also
    --------
    beatnum.lib.numsetsetops : Module with a number of other functions for
                            perforget_ming set operations on numsets.
    duplicate : Repeat elements of an numset.

    Notes
    -----
    When an axis is specified the subnumsets indexed by the axis are sorted.
    This is done by making the specified axis the first dimension of the numset
    (move the axis to the first dimension to keep the order of the other axes)
    and then convert_into_one_diget_ming the subnumsets in C order. The convert_into_one_dimed subnumsets are
    then viewed as a structured type with each element given a label, with the
    effect that we end up with a 1-D numset of structured types that can be
    treated in the same way as any_condition other 1-D numset. The result is that the
    convert_into_one_dimed subnumsets are sorted in lexicographic order starting with the
    first element.

    .. versionchanged: NumPy 1.21
        If nan values are in the ibnut numset, a single nan is put
        to the end of the sorted uniq values.

        Also for complex numsets all NaN values are considered equivalent
        (no matter whether the NaN is in the reality or imaginaryinary part).
        As the representant for the returned numset the smallest one in the
        lexicographical order is chosen - see bn.sort for how the lexicographical
        order is defined for complex numsets.

vectorisation(pyfunc, otypes=None, doc=None, excluded=None, cache=False, signature=None):
    vectorisation(pyfunc, otypes=None, doc=None, excluded=None, cache=False,
              signature=None)

    Generalized function class.

    Define a vectorisationd function which takes a nested sequence of objects or
    beatnum numsets as ibnuts and returns a single beatnum numset or a tuple of beatnum
    numsets. The vectorisationd function evaluates `pyfunc` over successive tuples
    of the ibnut numsets like the python map function, except it uses the
    broadcasting rules of beatnum.

    The data type of the output of `vectorisationd` is deterget_mined by calling
    the function with the first element of the ibnut.  This can be avoided
    by specifying the `otypes` argument.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pyfunc : callable
        A python function or method.
    otypes : str or list of dtypes, optional
        The output data type. It must be specified as either a string of
        typecode characters or a list of data type specifiers. There should
        be one data type specifier for each output.
    doc : str, optional
        The docstring for the function. If None, the docstring will be the
        ``pyfunc.__doc__``.
    excluded : set, optional
        Set of strings or integers representing the positional or keyword
        arguments for which the function will not be vectorisationd.  These will be
        passed directly to `pyfunc` unmodified.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

    cache : bool, optional
        If `True`, then cache the first function call that deterget_mines the number
        of outputs if `otypes` is not provided.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

    signature : string, optional
        Generalized universal function signature, e.g., ``(m,n),(n)->(m)`` for
        vectorisationd matrix-vector multiplication. If provided, ``pyfunc`` will
        be called with (and expected to return) numsets with shapes given by the
        size of corresponding core dimensions. By default, ``pyfunc`` is
        assumed to take scalars as ibnut and output.

        .. versionadded:: 1.12.0

    Returns
    -------
    vectorisationd : callable
        Vectorized function.

    See Also
    --------
    frompyfunc : Takes an arbitrary Python function and returns a ufunc

    Notes
    -----
    The `vectorisation` function is provided primarily for convenience, not for
    performance. The implementation is essentially a for loop.

    If `otypes` is not specified, then a call to the function with the
    first argument will be used to deterget_mine the number of outputs.  The
    results of this call will be cached if `cache` is `True` to prevent
    calling the function twice.  However, to implement the cache, the
    original function must be wrapped which will slow down subsequent
    calls, so only do this if your function is expensive.

    The new keyword argument interface and `excluded` argument support
    further degrades performance.

    References
    ----------
    .. [1] :doc:`/reference/c-api/generalized-ufuncs`

        the subnumsets indexed by the given axis will be convert_into_one_dimed and treated
        as the elements of a 1-D numset with the dimension of the given axis,
        see the notes for more details.  Object numsets or structured numsets
        that contain objects are not supported if the `axis` kwarg is used. The
        default is None.

change_shape_to(a, newshape, order='C'):
    Gives a new shape to an numset without changing its data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Array to be change_shape_tod.
    newshape : int or tuple of ints
        The new shape should be compatible with the original shape. If
        an integer, then the result will be a 1-D numset of that length.
        One shape dimension can be -1. In this case, the value is
        inferred from the length of the numset and remaining dimensions.
    order : {'C', 'F', 'A'}, optional
        Read the elements of `a` using this index order, and place the
        elements into the change_shape_tod numset using this index order.  'C'
        averages to read / write the elements using C-like index order,
        with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first
        axis index changing slowest. 'F' averages to read / write the
        elements using Fortran-like index order, with the first index
        changing fastest, and the last index changing slowest. Note that
        the 'C' and 'F' options take no account of the memory layout of
        the underlying numset, and only refer to the order of indexing.
        'A' averages to read / write the elements in Fortran-like index
        order if `a` is Fortran *contiguous* in memory, C-like order
        otherwise.

    Returns
    -------
    change_shape_tod_numset : ndnumset
        This will be a new view object if possible; otherwise, it will
        be a copy.  Note there is no guarantee of the *memory layout* (C- or
        Fortran- contiguous) of the returned numset.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.change_shape_to : Equivalent method.

    Notes
    -----
    It is not always possible to change the shape of an numset without
    copying the data. If you want an error to be raised when the data is copied,
    you should assign the new shape to the shape attribute of the numset::

     >>> a = bn.zeros((10, 2))

     # A switching_places makes the numset non-contiguous
     >>> b = a.T

     # Taking a view makes it possible to modify the shape without modifying
     # the initial object.
     >>> c = b.view()
     >>> c.shape = (20)
     Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
     AttributeError: Incompatible shape for in-place modification. Use
     `.change_shape_to()` to make a copy with the desired shape.

    The `order` keyword gives the index ordering both for *fetching* the values
    from `a`, and then *placing* the values into the output numset.
    For example, let's say you have an numset:

    >>> a = bn.arr_range(6).change_shape_to((3, 2))
    >>> a
    numset([[0, 1],
           [2, 3],
           [4, 5]])

    You can think of reshaping as first asviewing the numset (using the given
    index order), then sticking the elements from the asviewed numset into the
    new numset using the same kind of index ordering as was used for the
    asviewing.

    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3)) # C-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a), (2, 3)) # equivalent to C asview then C change_shape_to
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3), order='F') # Fortran-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a, order='F'), (2, 3), order='F')
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])

difference(a, n=1, axis=-1, prepend=<no value>, apd=<no value>):
    Calculate the n-th discrete differenceerence along the given axis.

    The first differenceerence is given by ``out[i] = a[i+1] - a[i]`` along
    the given axis, higher differenceerences are calculated by using `difference`
    recursively.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Ibnut numset
    n : int, optional
        The number of times values are differenceerenced. If zero, the ibnut
        is returned as-is.
    axis : int, optional
        The axis along which the differenceerence is taken, default is the
        last axis.
    prepend, apd : numset_like, optional
        Values to prepend or apd to `a` along axis prior to
        perforget_ming the differenceerence.  Scalar values are expanded to
        numsets with length 1 in the direction of axis and the shape
        of the ibnut numset in along all other axes.  Otherwise the
        dimension and shape must match `a` except along axis.

        .. versionadded:: 1.16.0

    Returns
    -------
    difference : ndnumset
        The n-th differenceerences. The shape of the output is the same as `a`
        except along `axis` filter_condition the dimension is smaller by `n`. The
        type of the output is the same as the type of the differenceerence
        between any_condition two elements of `a`. This is the same as the type of
        `a` in most cases. A notable exception is `datetime64`, which
        results in a `timedelta64` output numset.

    See Also
    --------
    gradient, edifference1d, cumsum

    Notes
    -----
    Type is preserved for boolean numsets, so the result will contain
    `False` when consecutive elements are the same and `True` when they
    differenceer.

    For unsigned integer numsets, the results will also be unsigned. This
    should not be surprising, as the result is consistent with
    calculating the differenceerence directly:

    >>> u8_arr = bn.numset([1, 0], dtype=bn.uint8)
    >>> bn.difference(u8_arr)
    numset([255], dtype=uint8)
    >>> u8_arr[1,...] - u8_arr[0,...]
    255

    If this is not desirable, then the numset should be cast to a larger
    integer type first:

    >>> i16_arr = u8_arr.convert_type(bn.int16)
    >>> bn.difference(i16_arr)
    numset([-1], dtype=int16)

    Return evenly spaced values within a given interval.

    Values are generated within the half-open interval ``[start, stop)``
    (in other words, the interval including `start` but excluding `stop`).
    For integer arguments the function is equivalent to the Python built-in
    `range` function, but returns an ndnumset rather than a list.

    When using a non-integer step, such as 0.1, the results will often not
    be consistent.  It is better to use `beatnum.linspace` for these cases.

    Parameters
    ----------
    start : integer or reality, optional
        Start of interval.  The interval includes this value.  The default
        start value is 0.
    stop : integer or reality
        End of interval.  The interval does not include this value, except
        in some cases filter_condition `step` is not an integer and floating point
        round-off affects the length of `out`.
    step : integer or reality, optional
        Spacing between values.  For any_condition output `out`, this is the distance
        between two adjacent values, ``out[i+1] - out[i]``.  The default
        step size is 1.  If `step` is specified as a position argument,
        `start` must also be given.
    dtype : dtype
        The type of the output numset.  If `dtype` is not given, infer the data
        type from the other ibnut arguments.
    like : numset_like
        Reference object to allow the creation of numsets which are not
        NumPy numsets. If an numset-like passed in as ``like`` supports
        the ``__numset_function__`` protocol, the result will be defined
        by it. In this case, it ensures the creation of an numset object
        compatible with that passed in via this argument.

        .. versionadded:: 1.20.0

    Returns
    -------
    arr_range : ndnumset
        Array of evenly spaced values.

        For floating point arguments, the length of the result is
        ``ceil((stop - start)/step)``.  Because of floating point overflow,
        this rule may result in the last element of `out` being greater
        than `stop`.

    See Also
    --------
    beatnum.linspace : Evenly spaced numbers with careful handling of endpoints.
    beatnum.ogrid: Arrays of evenly spaced numbers in N-dimensions.
    beatnum.mgrid: Grid-shaped numsets of evenly spaced numbers in N-dimensions.

change_shape_to(a, newshape, order='C'):
    Gives a new shape to an numset without changing its data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Array to be change_shape_tod.
    newshape : int or tuple of ints
        The new shape should be compatible with the original shape. If
        an integer, then the result will be a 1-D numset of that length.
        One shape dimension can be -1. In this case, the value is
        inferred from the length of the numset and remaining dimensions.
    order : {'C', 'F', 'A'}, optional
        Read the elements of `a` using this index order, and place the
        elements into the change_shape_tod numset using this index order.  'C'
        averages to read / write the elements using C-like index order,
        with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first
        axis index changing slowest. 'F' averages to read / write the
        elements using Fortran-like index order, with the first index
        changing fastest, and the last index changing slowest. Note that
        the 'C' and 'F' options take no account of the memory layout of
        the underlying numset, and only refer to the order of indexing.
        'A' averages to read / write the elements in Fortran-like index
        order if `a` is Fortran *contiguous* in memory, C-like order
        otherwise.

    Returns
    -------
    change_shape_tod_numset : ndnumset
        This will be a new view object if possible; otherwise, it will
        be a copy.  Note there is no guarantee of the *memory layout* (C- or
        Fortran- contiguous) of the returned numset.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.change_shape_to : Equivalent method.

    Notes
    -----
    It is not always possible to change the shape of an numset without
    copying the data. If you want an error to be raised when the data is copied,
    you should assign the new shape to the shape attribute of the numset::

     >>> a = bn.zeros((10, 2))

     # A switching_places makes the numset non-contiguous
     >>> b = a.T

     # Taking a view makes it possible to modify the shape without modifying
     # the initial object.
     >>> c = b.view()
     >>> c.shape = (20)
     Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
     AttributeError: Incompatible shape for in-place modification. Use
     `.change_shape_to()` to make a copy with the desired shape.

    The `order` keyword gives the index ordering both for *fetching* the values
    from `a`, and then *placing* the values into the output numset.
    For example, let's say you have an numset:

    >>> a = bn.arr_range(6).change_shape_to((3, 2))
    >>> a
    numset([[0, 1],
           [2, 3],
           [4, 5]])

    You can think of reshaping as first asviewing the numset (using the given
    index order), then sticking the elements from the asviewed numset into the
    new numset using the same kind of index ordering as was used for the
    asviewing.

    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3)) # C-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a), (2, 3)) # equivalent to C asview then C change_shape_to
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3), order='F') # Fortran-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a, order='F'), (2, 3), order='F')
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])

    Return evenly spaced values within a given interval.

    Values are generated within the half-open interval ``[start, stop)``
    (in other words, the interval including `start` but excluding `stop`).
    For integer arguments the function is equivalent to the Python built-in
    `range` function, but returns an ndnumset rather than a list.

    When using a non-integer step, such as 0.1, the results will often not
    be consistent.  It is better to use `beatnum.linspace` for these cases.

        start value is 0.
    stop : integer or reality

        in some cases filter_condition `step` is not an integer and floating point
        round-off affects the length of `out`.
    step : integer or reality, optional
        Spacing between values.  For any_condition output `out`, this is the distance
        between two adjacent values, ``out[i+1] - out[i]``.  The default
        step size is 1.  If `step` is specified as a position argument,
        `start` must also be given.
    dtype : dtype
        The type of the output numset.  If `dtype` is not given, infer the data
        type from the other ibnut arguments.
    like : numset_like
        Reference object to allow the creation of numsets which are not
        NumPy numsets. If an numset-like passed in as ``like`` supports
        the ``__numset_function__`` protocol, the result will be defined
        by it. In this case, it ensures the creation of an numset object
        compatible with that passed in via this argument.

        .. versionadded:: 1.20.0

    Returns
    -------
    arr_range : ndnumset
        Array of evenly spaced values.

        For floating point arguments, the length of the result is
        ``ceil((stop - start)/step)``.  Because of floating point overflow,
        this rule may result in the last element of `out` being greater
        than `stop`.

    Compute the hist_operation of a dataset.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Ibnut data. The hist_operation is computed over the convert_into_one_dimed numset.
    bins : int or sequence of scalars or str, optional
        If `bins` is an int, it defines the number of equal-width
        bins in the given range (10, by default). If `bins` is a
        sequence, it defines a monotonically increasing numset of bin edges,
        including the rightmost edge, allowing for non-uniform bin widths.

        .. versionadded:: 1.11.0

        If `bins` is a string, it defines the method used to calculate the
        optimal bin width, as defined by `hist_operation_bin_edges`.

    range : (float, float), optional
        The lower and upper range of the bins.  If not provided, range
        is simply ``(a.get_min(), a.get_max())``.  Values outside the range are
        ignored. The first element of the range must be less than or
        equal to the second. `range` affects the automatic bin
        computation as well. While bin width is computed to be optimal
        based on the actual data within `range`, the bin count will fill
        the entire range including portions containing no data.
    normlizattioned : bool, optional

        .. deprecated:: 1.6.0

        This is equivalent to the `density` argument, but produces incorrect
        results for unequal bin widths. It should not be used.

        .. versionchanged:: 1.15.0
            DeprecationWarnings are actually emitted.

    weights : numset_like, optional
        An numset of weights, of the same shape as `a`.  Each value in
        `a` only contributes its associated weight towards the bin count
        (instead of 1). If `density` is True, the weights are
        normlizattionalized, so that the integral of the density over the range
        remains 1.
    density : bool, optional
        If ``False``, the result will contain the number of samples in
        each bin. If ``True``, the result is the value of the
        probability *density* function at the bin, normlizattionalized such that
        the *integral* over the range is 1. Note that the sum of the
        hist_operation values will not be equal to 1 unless bins of unity
        width are chosen; it is not a probability *mass* function.

        Overrides the ``normlizattioned`` keyword if given.

    Returns
    -------
    hist : numset
        The values of the hist_operation. See `density` and `weights` for a
        description of the possible semantics.
    bin_edges : numset of dtype float
        Return the bin edges ``(length(hist)+1)``.


    See Also
    --------
    hist_operationdd, binoccurrence, find_sorted, digitize, hist_operation_bin_edges

    Notes
    -----
    All but the last (righthand-most) bin is half-open.  In other words,
    if `bins` is::

      [1, 2, 3, 4]

    then the first bin is ``[1, 2)`` (including 1, but excluding 2) and
    the second ``[2, 3)``.  The last bin, however, is ``[3, 4]``, which
    *includes* 4.

find_sorted(a, v, side='left', sorter=None):
    Find indices filter_condition elements should be sticked to maintain order.

    Find the indices into a sorted numset `a` such that, if the
    corresponding elements in `v` were sticked before the indices, the
    order of `a` would be preserved.

    Assuming that `a` is sorted:

    ======  ============================
    `side`  returned index `i` satisfies
    ======  ============================
    left    ``a[i-1] < v <= a[i]``
    right   ``a[i-1] <= v < a[i]``
    ======  ============================

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : 1-D numset_like
        Ibnut numset. If `sorter` is None, then it must be sorted in
        ascending order, otherwise `sorter` must be an numset of indices
        that sort it.
    v : numset_like
        Values to stick into `a`.
    side : {'left', 'right'}, optional
        If 'left', the index of the first suitable location found is given.
        If 'right', return the last such index.  If there is no suitable
        index, return either 0 or N (filter_condition N is the length of `a`).
    sorter : 1-D numset_like, optional
        Optional numset of integer indices that sort numset a into ascending
        order. They are typically the result of argsort.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

    Returns
    -------
    indices : numset of ints
        Array of stickion points with the same shape as `v`.

    See Also
    --------
    sort : Return a sorted copy of an numset.
    hist_operation : Produce hist_operation from 1-D data.

    Notes
    -----
    Binary search is used to find the required stickion points.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like

    newshape : int or tuple of ints

        inferred from the length of the numset and remaining dimensions.

        elements into the change_shape_tod numset using this index order.  'C'
        averages to read / write the elements using C-like index order,
        with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first
        axis index changing slowest. 'F' averages to read / write the
        elements using Fortran-like index order, with the first index
        changing fastest, and the last index changing slowest. Note that
        the 'C' and 'F' options take no account of the memory layout of
        the underlying numset, and only refer to the order of indexing.
        'A' averages to read / write the elements in Fortran-like index
        order if `a` is Fortran *contiguous* in memory, C-like order
        otherwise.

        be a copy.  Note there is no guarantee of the *memory layout* (C- or
        Fortran- contiguous) of the returned numset.

    copying the data. If you want an error to be raised when the data is copied,

     # the initial object.

     `.change_shape_to()` to make a copy with the desired shape.

vectorisation(pyfunc, otypes=None, doc=None, excluded=None, cache=False, signature=None):
    vectorisation(pyfunc, otypes=None, doc=None, excluded=None, cache=False,
              signature=None)

    Generalized function class.

    Define a vectorisationd function which takes a nested sequence of objects or
    beatnum numsets as ibnuts and returns a single beatnum numset or a tuple of beatnum
    numsets. The vectorisationd function evaluates `pyfunc` over successive tuples
    of the ibnut numsets like the python map function, except it uses the
    broadcasting rules of beatnum.

    The data type of the output of `vectorisationd` is deterget_mined by calling
    the function with the first element of the ibnut.  This can be avoided
    by specifying the `otypes` argument.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pyfunc : callable
        A python function or method.
    otypes : str or list of dtypes, optional
        The output data type. It must be specified as either a string of
        typecode characters or a list of data type specifiers. There should
        be one data type specifier for each output.
    doc : str, optional
        The docstring for the function. If None, the docstring will be the
        ``pyfunc.__doc__``.
    excluded : set, optional
        Set of strings or integers representing the positional or keyword
        arguments for which the function will not be vectorisationd.  These will be
        passed directly to `pyfunc` unmodified.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

    cache : bool, optional
        If `True`, then cache the first function call that deterget_mines the number
        of outputs if `otypes` is not provided.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

    signature : string, optional
        Generalized universal function signature, e.g., ``(m,n),(n)->(m)`` for
        vectorisationd matrix-vector multiplication. If provided, ``pyfunc`` will
        be called with (and expected to return) numsets with shapes given by the
        size of corresponding core dimensions. By default, ``pyfunc`` is
        assumed to take scalars as ibnut and output.

        .. versionadded:: 1.12.0

    Returns
    -------
    vectorisationd : callable
        Vectorized function.

    See Also
    --------
    frompyfunc : Takes an arbitrary Python function and returns a ufunc

    Notes
    -----
    The `vectorisation` function is provided primarily for convenience, not for
    performance. The implementation is essentially a for loop.

    If `otypes` is not specified, then a call to the function with the
    first argument will be used to deterget_mine the number of outputs.  The
    results of this call will be cached if `cache` is `True` to prevent
    calling the function twice.  However, to implement the cache, the
    original function must be wrapped which will slow down subsequent
    calls, so only do this if your function is expensive.

    The new keyword argument interface and `excluded` argument support
    further degrades performance.

    References
    ----------
    .. [1] :doc:`/reference/c-api/generalized-ufuncs`

total_count(a, axis=None, dtype=None, out=None, keepdims=<no value>, initial=<no value>, where=<no value>):
    Sum of numset elements over a given axis.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Elements to sum.
    axis : None or int or tuple of ints, optional
        Axis or axes along which a sum is performed.  The default,
        axis=None, will sum total of the elements of the ibnut numset.  If
        axis is negative it counts from the last to the first axis.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

        If axis is a tuple of ints, a total_count is performed on total of the axes
        specified in the tuple instead of a single axis or total the axes as
        before.
    dtype : dtype, optional
        The type of the returned numset and of the accumulator in which the
        elements are summed.  The dtype of `a` is used by default unless `a`
        has an integer dtype of less precision than the default platform
        integer.  In that case, if `a` is signed then the platform integer
        is used while if `a` is unsigned then an unsigned integer of the
        same precision as the platform integer is used.
    out : ndnumset, optional
        Alternative output numset in which to place the result. It must have
        the same shape as the expected output, but the type of the output
        values will be cast if necessary.
    keepdims : bool, optional
        If this is set to True, the axes which are reduced are left
        in the result as dimensions with size one. With this option,
        the result will broadcast correctly against the ibnut numset.

        If the default value is passed, then `keepdims` will not be
        passed through to the `total_count` method of sub-classes of
        `ndnumset`, however any_condition non-default value will be.  If the
        sub-class' method does not implement `keepdims` any_condition
        exceptions will be raised.
    initial : scalar, optional
        Starting value for the sum. See `~beatnum.ufunc.reduce` for details.

        .. versionadded:: 1.15.0

    filter_condition : numset_like of bool, optional
        Elements to include in the total_count. See `~beatnum.ufunc.reduce` for details.

        .. versionadded:: 1.17.0

    Returns
    -------
    total_count_along_axis : ndnumset
        An numset with the same shape as `a`, with the specified
        axis removed.   If `a` is a 0-d numset, or if `axis` is None, a scalar
        is returned.  If an output numset is specified, a reference to
        `out` is returned.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.total_count : Equivalent method.

    add_concat.reduce : Equivalent functionality of `add_concat`.

    cumsum : Cumulative sum of numset elements.

    trapz : Integration of numset values using the composite trapezoidal rule.

    average, average

    Notes
    -----
    Arithmetic is modular when using integer types, and no error is
    raised on overflow.

    The sum of an empty numset is the neutral element 0:

    >>> bn.total_count([])
    0.0

    For floating point numbers the numerical precision of sum (and
    ``bn.add_concat.reduce``) is in general limited by directly add_concating each number
    individutotaly to the result causing rounding errors in every step.
    However, often beatnum will use a  numerically better approach (partial
    pairwise summation) leading to improved precision in many_condition use-cases.
    This improved precision is always provided when no ``axis`` is given.
    When ``axis`` is given, it will depend on which axis is summed.
    Technically, to provide the best speed possible, the improved precision
    is only used when the summation is along the fast axis in memory.
    Note that the exact precision may vary depending on other parameters.
    In contrast to NumPy, Python's ``math.fsum`` function uses a slower but
    more precise approach to summation.
    Especially when summing a large number of lower precision floating point
    numbers, such as ``float32``, numerical errors can become significant.
    In such cases it can be advisable to use `dtype="float64"` to use a higher
    precision for the output.

total_count(a, axis=None, dtype=None, out=None, keepdims=<no value>, initial=<no value>, where=<no value>):
    Sum of numset elements over a given axis.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Elements to sum.
    axis : None or int or tuple of ints, optional
        Axis or axes along which a sum is performed.  The default,
        axis=None, will sum total of the elements of the ibnut numset.  If
        axis is negative it counts from the last to the first axis.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

        If axis is a tuple of ints, a total_count is performed on total of the axes
        specified in the tuple instead of a single axis or total the axes as
        before.
    dtype : dtype, optional
        The type of the returned numset and of the accumulator in which the
        elements are summed.  The dtype of `a` is used by default unless `a`
        has an integer dtype of less precision than the default platform
        integer.  In that case, if `a` is signed then the platform integer
        is used while if `a` is unsigned then an unsigned integer of the
        same precision as the platform integer is used.
    out : ndnumset, optional
        Alternative output numset in which to place the result. It must have
        the same shape as the expected output, but the type of the output
        values will be cast if necessary.
    keepdims : bool, optional
        If this is set to True, the axes which are reduced are left
        in the result as dimensions with size one. With this option,
        the result will broadcast correctly against the ibnut numset.

        If the default value is passed, then `keepdims` will not be
        passed through to the `total_count` method of sub-classes of
        `ndnumset`, however any_condition non-default value will be.  If the
        sub-class' method does not implement `keepdims` any_condition
        exceptions will be raised.
    initial : scalar, optional
        Starting value for the sum. See `~beatnum.ufunc.reduce` for details.

        .. versionadded:: 1.15.0

    filter_condition : numset_like of bool, optional
        Elements to include in the total_count. See `~beatnum.ufunc.reduce` for details.

        .. versionadded:: 1.17.0

    Returns
    -------
    total_count_along_axis : ndnumset
        An numset with the same shape as `a`, with the specified
        axis removed.   If `a` is a 0-d numset, or if `axis` is None, a scalar
        is returned.  If an output numset is specified, a reference to
        `out` is returned.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.total_count : Equivalent method.

    add_concat.reduce : Equivalent functionality of `add_concat`.

    cumsum : Cumulative sum of numset elements.

    trapz : Integration of numset values using the composite trapezoidal rule.

    average, average

    Notes
    -----
    Arithmetic is modular when using integer types, and no error is
    raised on overflow.

    The sum of an empty numset is the neutral element 0:

    >>> bn.total_count([])
    0.0

    ``bn.add_concat.reduce``) is in general limited by directly add_concating each number
    individutotaly to the result causing rounding errors in every step.
    However, often beatnum will use a  numerically better approach (partial
    pairwise summation) leading to improved precision in many_condition use-cases.
    This improved precision is always provided when no ``axis`` is given.

    is only used when the summation is along the fast axis in memory.
    Note that the exact precision may vary depending on other parameters.

    more precise approach to summation.

    numbers, such as ``float32``, numerical errors can become significant.
    In such cases it can be advisable to use `dtype="float64"` to use a higher
    precision for the output.

    Return evenly spaced values within a given interval.

    Values are generated within the half-open interval ``[start, stop)``
    (in other words, the interval including `start` but excluding `stop`).

    `range` function, but returns an ndnumset rather than a list.

    be consistent.  It is better to use `beatnum.linspace` for these cases.

    ----------

        start value is 0.
    stop : integer or reality

        in some cases filter_condition `step` is not an integer and floating point
        round-off affects the length of `out`.
    step : integer or reality, optional
        Spacing between values.  For any_condition output `out`, this is the distance
        between two adjacent values, ``out[i+1] - out[i]``.  The default
        step size is 1.  If `step` is specified as a position argument,
        `start` must also be given.
    dtype : dtype
        The type of the output numset.  If `dtype` is not given, infer the data
        type from the other ibnut arguments.

        NumPy numsets. If an numset-like passed in as ``like`` supports
        the ``__numset_function__`` protocol, the result will be defined
        by it. In this case, it ensures the creation of an numset object
        compatible with that passed in via this argument.

        .. versionadded:: 1.20.0

    Returns

        For floating point arguments, the length of the result is
        ``ceil((stop - start)/step)``.  Because of floating point overflow,
        this rule may result in the last element of `out` being greater
        than `stop`.

change_shape_to(a, newshape, order='C'):
    Gives a new shape to an numset without changing its data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Array to be change_shape_tod.
    newshape : int or tuple of ints
        The new shape should be compatible with the original shape. If
        an integer, then the result will be a 1-D numset of that length.
        One shape dimension can be -1. In this case, the value is
        inferred from the length of the numset and remaining dimensions.
    order : {'C', 'F', 'A'}, optional
        Read the elements of `a` using this index order, and place the
        elements into the change_shape_tod numset using this index order.  'C'
        averages to read / write the elements using C-like index order,
        with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first
        axis index changing slowest. 'F' averages to read / write the
        elements using Fortran-like index order, with the first index
        changing fastest, and the last index changing slowest. Note that
        the 'C' and 'F' options take no account of the memory layout of
        the underlying numset, and only refer to the order of indexing.
        'A' averages to read / write the elements in Fortran-like index
        order if `a` is Fortran *contiguous* in memory, C-like order
        otherwise.

    Returns
    -------
    change_shape_tod_numset : ndnumset
        This will be a new view object if possible; otherwise, it will
        be a copy.  Note there is no guarantee of the *memory layout* (C- or
        Fortran- contiguous) of the returned numset.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.change_shape_to : Equivalent method.

    Notes
    -----
    It is not always possible to change the shape of an numset without
    copying the data. If you want an error to be raised when the data is copied,
    you should assign the new shape to the shape attribute of the numset::

     >>> a = bn.zeros((10, 2))

     # A switching_places makes the numset non-contiguous
     >>> b = a.T

     # Taking a view makes it possible to modify the shape without modifying
     # the initial object.
     >>> c = b.view()
     >>> c.shape = (20)
     Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
     AttributeError: Incompatible shape for in-place modification. Use
     `.change_shape_to()` to make a copy with the desired shape.

    The `order` keyword gives the index ordering both for *fetching* the values
    from `a`, and then *placing* the values into the output numset.
    For example, let's say you have an numset:

    >>> a = bn.arr_range(6).change_shape_to((3, 2))
    >>> a
    numset([[0, 1],
           [2, 3],
           [4, 5]])

    You can think of reshaping as first asviewing the numset (using the given
    index order), then sticking the elements from the asviewed numset into the
    new numset using the same kind of index ordering as was used for the
    asviewing.

        equal to the second. `range` affects the automatic bin
        computation as well. While bin width is computed to be optimal
        based on the actual data within `range`, the bin count will fill
        the entire range including portions containing no data.

        results for unequal bin widths. It should not be used.

        `a` only contributes its associated weight towards the bin count
        (instead of 1). If `density` is True, the weights are
        normlizattionalized, so that the integral of the density over the range
        remains 1.
    density : bool, optional

        each bin. If ``True``, the result is the value of the
        probability *density* function at the bin, normlizattionalized such that
        the *integral* over the range is 1. Note that the sum of the
        hist_operation values will not be equal to 1 unless bins of unity
        width are chosen; it is not a probability *mass* function.

        Overrides the ``normlizattioned`` keyword if given.

    -------
    hist : numset
        The values of the hist_operation. See `density` and `weights` for a
        description of the possible semantics.
    bin_edges : numset of dtype float

    the second ``[2, 3)``.  The last bin, however, is ``[3, 4]``, which
    *includes* 4.

change_shape_to(a, newshape, order='C'):
    Gives a new shape to an numset without changing its data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Array to be change_shape_tod.
    newshape : int or tuple of ints
        The new shape should be compatible with the original shape. If
        an integer, then the result will be a 1-D numset of that length.
        One shape dimension can be -1. In this case, the value is
        inferred from the length of the numset and remaining dimensions.
    order : {'C', 'F', 'A'}, optional
        Read the elements of `a` using this index order, and place the
        elements into the change_shape_tod numset using this index order.  'C'
        averages to read / write the elements using C-like index order,
        with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first
        axis index changing slowest. 'F' averages to read / write the
        elements using Fortran-like index order, with the first index
        changing fastest, and the last index changing slowest. Note that
        the 'C' and 'F' options take no account of the memory layout of
        the underlying numset, and only refer to the order of indexing.
        'A' averages to read / write the elements in Fortran-like index
        order if `a` is Fortran *contiguous* in memory, C-like order
        otherwise.

    Returns
    -------
    change_shape_tod_numset : ndnumset
        This will be a new view object if possible; otherwise, it will
        be a copy.  Note there is no guarantee of the *memory layout* (C- or
        Fortran- contiguous) of the returned numset.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.change_shape_to : Equivalent method.

    Notes
    -----
    It is not always possible to change the shape of an numset without
    copying the data. If you want an error to be raised when the data is copied,
    you should assign the new shape to the shape attribute of the numset::

     >>> a = bn.zeros((10, 2))

     # A switching_places makes the numset non-contiguous
     >>> b = a.T

     # Taking a view makes it possible to modify the shape without modifying
     # the initial object.
     >>> c = b.view()
     >>> c.shape = (20)
     Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
     AttributeError: Incompatible shape for in-place modification. Use
     `.change_shape_to()` to make a copy with the desired shape.

    The `order` keyword gives the index ordering both for *fetching* the values
    from `a`, and then *placing* the values into the output numset.
    For example, let's say you have an numset:

    >>> a = bn.arr_range(6).change_shape_to((3, 2))
    >>> a
    numset([[0, 1],
           [2, 3],
           [4, 5]])

    You can think of reshaping as first asviewing the numset (using the given
    index order), then sticking the elements from the asviewed numset into the
    new numset using the same kind of index ordering as was used for the
    asviewing.

    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3)) # C-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a), (2, 3)) # equivalent to C asview then C change_shape_to
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3), order='F') # Fortran-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a, order='F'), (2, 3), order='F')
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])

change_shape_to(a, newshape, order='C'):
    Gives a new shape to an numset without changing its data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Array to be change_shape_tod.
    newshape : int or tuple of ints
        The new shape should be compatible with the original shape. If
        an integer, then the result will be a 1-D numset of that length.
        One shape dimension can be -1. In this case, the value is
        inferred from the length of the numset and remaining dimensions.
    order : {'C', 'F', 'A'}, optional
        Read the elements of `a` using this index order, and place the
        elements into the change_shape_tod numset using this index order.  'C'
        averages to read / write the elements using C-like index order,
        with the last axis index changing fastest, back to the first
        axis index changing slowest. 'F' averages to read / write the
        elements using Fortran-like index order, with the first index
        changing fastest, and the last index changing slowest. Note that
        the 'C' and 'F' options take no account of the memory layout of
        the underlying numset, and only refer to the order of indexing.
        'A' averages to read / write the elements in Fortran-like index
        order if `a` is Fortran *contiguous* in memory, C-like order
        otherwise.

    Returns
    -------
    change_shape_tod_numset : ndnumset
        This will be a new view object if possible; otherwise, it will
        be a copy.  Note there is no guarantee of the *memory layout* (C- or
        Fortran- contiguous) of the returned numset.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.change_shape_to : Equivalent method.

    Notes
    -----
    It is not always possible to change the shape of an numset without
    copying the data. If you want an error to be raised when the data is copied,
    you should assign the new shape to the shape attribute of the numset::

     >>> a = bn.zeros((10, 2))

     # A switching_places makes the numset non-contiguous
     >>> b = a.T

     # Taking a view makes it possible to modify the shape without modifying
     # the initial object.
     >>> c = b.view()
     >>> c.shape = (20)
     Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
     AttributeError: Incompatible shape for in-place modification. Use
     `.change_shape_to()` to make a copy with the desired shape.

    The `order` keyword gives the index ordering both for *fetching* the values
    from `a`, and then *placing* the values into the output numset.
    For example, let's say you have an numset:

    >>> a = bn.arr_range(6).change_shape_to((3, 2))
    >>> a
    numset([[0, 1],
           [2, 3],
           [4, 5]])

    You can think of reshaping as first asviewing the numset (using the given
    index order), then sticking the elements from the asviewed numset into the
    new numset using the same kind of index ordering as was used for the
    asviewing.

    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3)) # C-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a), (2, 3)) # equivalent to C asview then C change_shape_to
    numset([[0, 1, 2],
           [3, 4, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(a, (2, 3), order='F') # Fortran-like index ordering
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])
    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a, order='F'), (2, 3), order='F')
    numset([[0, 4, 3],
           [2, 1, 5]])

total_count(a, axis=None, dtype=None, out=None, keepdims=<no value>, initial=<no value>, where=<no value>):
    Sum of numset elements over a given axis.

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : numset_like
        Elements to sum.
    axis : None or int or tuple of ints, optional
        Axis or axes along which a sum is performed.  The default,
        axis=None, will sum total of the elements of the ibnut numset.  If
        axis is negative it counts from the last to the first axis.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

        If axis is a tuple of ints, a total_count is performed on total of the axes
        specified in the tuple instead of a single axis or total the axes as
        before.
    dtype : dtype, optional
        The type of the returned numset and of the accumulator in which the
        elements are summed.  The dtype of `a` is used by default unless `a`
        has an integer dtype of less precision than the default platform
        integer.  In that case, if `a` is signed then the platform integer
        is used while if `a` is unsigned then an unsigned integer of the
        same precision as the platform integer is used.
    out : ndnumset, optional
        Alternative output numset in which to place the result. It must have
        the same shape as the expected output, but the type of the output
        values will be cast if necessary.
    keepdims : bool, optional
        If this is set to True, the axes which are reduced are left
        in the result as dimensions with size one. With this option,
        the result will broadcast correctly against the ibnut numset.

        If the default value is passed, then `keepdims` will not be
        passed through to the `total_count` method of sub-classes of
        `ndnumset`, however any_condition non-default value will be.  If the
        sub-class' method does not implement `keepdims` any_condition
        exceptions will be raised.
    initial : scalar, optional
        Starting value for the sum. See `~beatnum.ufunc.reduce` for details.

        .. versionadded:: 1.15.0

    filter_condition : numset_like of bool, optional
        Elements to include in the total_count. See `~beatnum.ufunc.reduce` for details.

        .. versionadded:: 1.17.0

    Returns
    -------
    total_count_along_axis : ndnumset
        An numset with the same shape as `a`, with the specified
        axis removed.   If `a` is a 0-d numset, or if `axis` is None, a scalar
        is returned.  If an output numset is specified, a reference to
        `out` is returned.

    See Also
    --------
    ndnumset.total_count : Equivalent method.

    add_concat.reduce : Equivalent functionality of `add_concat`.

    cumsum : Cumulative sum of numset elements.

    trapz : Integration of numset values using the composite trapezoidal rule.

    average, average

    Notes
    -----
    Arithmetic is modular when using integer types, and no error is
    raised on overflow.

    The sum of an empty numset is the neutral element 0:

    >>> bn.total_count([])
    0.0

    For floating point numbers the numerical precision of sum (and
    ``bn.add_concat.reduce``) is in general limited by directly add_concating each number
    individutotaly to the result causing rounding errors in every step.
    However, often beatnum will use a  numerically better approach (partial
    pairwise summation) leading to improved precision in many_condition use-cases.
    This improved precision is always provided when no ``axis`` is given.
    When ``axis`` is given, it will depend on which axis is summed.
    Technically, to provide the best speed possible, the improved precision
    is only used when the summation is along the fast axis in memory.
    Note that the exact precision may vary depending on other parameters.
    In contrast to NumPy, Python's ``math.fsum`` function uses a slower but
    more precise approach to summation.
    Especially when summing a large number of lower precision floating point
    numbers, such as ``float32``, numerical errors can become significant.
    In such cases it can be advisable to use `dtype="float64"` to use a higher
    precision for the output.

    Parameters
    ----------

        axis index changing slowest. 'F' averages to read / write the
        elements using Fortran-like index order, with the first index
        changing fastest, and the last index changing slowest. Note that
        the 'C' and 'F' options take no account of the memory layout of

        'A' averages to read / write the elements in Fortran-like index
        order if `a` is Fortran *contiguous* in memory, C-like order

        be a copy.  Note there is no guarantee of the *memory layout* (C- or
        Fortran- contiguous) of the returned numset.

    copying the data. If you want an error to be raised when the data is copied,
    you should assign the new shape to the shape attribute of the numset::

     >>> a = bn.zeros((10, 2))

     # A switching_places makes the numset non-contiguous
     >>> b = a.T

     # Taking a view makes it possible to modify the shape without modifying
     # the initial object.
     >>> c = b.view()
     >>> c.shape = (20)
     Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
     AttributeError: Incompatible shape for in-place modification. Use
     `.change_shape_to()` to make a copy with the desired shape.

    from `a`, and then *placing* the values into the output numset.

    numset([[0, 1, 2],

    >>> bn.change_shape_to(bn.asview(a), (2, 3)) # equivalent to C asview then C change_shape_to
    numset([[0, 1, 2],

    numset([[0, 4, 3],

    numset([[0, 4, 3],

find_sorted(a, v, side='left', sorter=None):
    Find indices filter_condition elements should be sticked to maintain order.

    Find the indices into a sorted numset `a` such that, if the
    corresponding elements in `v` were sticked before the indices, the
    order of `a` would be preserved.

    Assuming that `a` is sorted:

    ======  ============================
    `side`  returned index `i` satisfies
    ======  ============================
    left    ``a[i-1] < v <= a[i]``
    right   ``a[i-1] <= v < a[i]``
    ======  ============================

    Parameters
    ----------
    a : 1-D numset_like
        Ibnut numset. If `sorter` is None, then it must be sorted in
        ascending order, otherwise `sorter` must be an numset of indices
        that sort it.
    v : numset_like
        Values to stick into `a`.
    side : {'left', 'right'}, optional
        If 'left', the index of the first suitable location found is given.
        If 'right', return the last such index.  If there is no suitable
        index, return either 0 or N (filter_condition N is the length of `a`).
    sorter : 1-D numset_like, optional
        Optional numset of integer indices that sort numset a into ascending
        order. They are typically the result of argsort.

        .. versionadded:: 1.7.0

    Returns
    -------
    indices : numset of ints
        Array of stickion points with the same shape as `v`.

    See Also
    --------
    sort : Return a sorted copy of an numset.
    hist_operation : Produce hist_operation from 1-D data.

    Notes
    -----
    Binary search is used to find the required stickion points.

    As of NumPy 1.4.0 `find_sorted` works with reality/complex numsets containing
    `nan` values. The enhanced sort order is documented in `sort`.

    This function uses the same algorithm as the builtin python `bisect.bisect_left`
    (``side='left'``) and `bisect.bisect_right` (``side='right'``) functions,
    which is also vectorisationd in the `v` argument.
